bus.ext.vocab.performance-objective.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.performance-objective.plain: A goal a business sets for how its operations should run, such as producing to a set standard, producing faster, producing more cheaply, or being able to change what it produces.
bus.ext.vocab.performance-objective.example: A bakery that promises bread on the shelf by six every morning has set speed as a performance objective.

bus.ext.vocab.operations-strategy.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.operations-strategy.plain: A deliberate change a business makes to how it produces, chosen because of what it wants its operations to achieve.
bus.ext.vocab.operations-strategy.example: Moving from ordering stock monthly to ordering it daily is an operations strategy.

bus.ext.vocab.defect.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.defect.plain: A unit of output that does not meet the standard the business set for it, so it has to be scrapped, remade or discounted.
bus.ext.vocab.defect.example: A shirt that leaves the line with a seam sewn open is a defect.

bus.ext.vocab.lead-time.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.lead-time.plain: The time between a business placing an order and the goods being available to use or sell.
bus.ext.vocab.lead-time.example: If a cafe orders beans on Monday and they arrive on Thursday, the lead time is three days.

bus.ext.vocab.carrying-cost.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.carrying-cost.plain: What it costs a business to hold stock it is not using yet: the space, the handling, the insurance, and the money tied up in it.
bus.ext.vocab.carrying-cost.example: A warehouse rented to hold spare parts is a carrying cost even in a month when no part is used.

bus.ext.vocab.non-core-process.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.non-core-process.plain: A process a business needs done but that is not the thing customers choose it for.
bus.ext.vocab.non-core-process.example: Payroll is a non-core process for a furniture maker.

bus.ext.vocab.changeover.subject: business_studies
bus.ext.vocab.changeover.plain: The work of switching a production line from making one thing to making another.
bus.ext.vocab.changeover.example: Resetting a bottling line from 600ml to 1.25 litre bottles is a changeover.

bus.ext.concept.quality-at-source.label: checking quality where the work happens

bus.ext.concept.time-and-stock.label: the relationship between how often you order and how much you hold

bus.ext.lesson.quality-at-source.title: Why checking earlier costs less than checking later

steps.text: Every business decides where in its process it looks for mistakes. It can look at the end, when the unit is finished, or it can look at each stage as the work is done.
A mistake found at the end has already had every later stage of work spent on it. A mistake found at the stage it happened has only had that stage spent on it.
So moving the check earlier does not make the workforce more careful. It changes how much work is thrown away when somebody is not.
A mistake is made at stage two of six. Where does the business lose less: finding it at stage three, or finding it at stage six?
steps.answer: At stage three, because only stage two's work has been spent on it.

steps.text: Stock sitting in a business is work it has already paid for and has not sold yet. It takes up space, it has to be handled, and the money spent on it cannot be spent on anything else.
Ordering in smaller amounts more often means less of it is sitting there at any moment, so the cost of holding it falls.
The cost of that is exposure. A business holding one day of stock has one day to fix a supplier who does not deliver, and a business holding one month has a month.
A business moves from ordering monthly to ordering weekly. What has it gained, and what has it given up?
steps.answer: It holds less stock, so carrying cost falls. It has less cover if a delivery is late.

question.subject: business_studies
question.text: Explain how operations strategies affect the quality, speed, cost and flexibility of a business's operations.
question.overallArgument: Each operations strategy changes something specific about how the business produces, and it is that change, rather than the intention behind it, that moves a performance objective.

relationship.intro: This question asks what an operations strategy actually does to the business, and which objective that change reaches.

claims.line: An operations strategy affects quality by changing something specific in how the business produces.
An operations strategy affects speed by changing something specific in how the business produces.
An operations strategy affects cost by changing something specific in how the business produces.
An operations strategy affects flexibility by changing something specific in how the business produces.

decode.verbMeaning: Explain means show how or why. For each objective you write about, the marker is looking for the step between the strategy and the objective, not just the pair of them.
decode.plainEnglish: Show how the things a business changes about the way it produces end up changing how well, how fast, how cheaply and how adaptably it produces.
decode.coreRelationship: A business changes something about how it produces, and that change moves one of the objectives it is measured on.

highlights.note: The changes the business makes. Each paragraph should name one.
How closely output matches the standard set for it.
How quickly the business can produce and deliver.
What it costs the business to produce a unit.
How easily the business can change what it produces.

cover.forEach: operations strategy → the specific change → the objective it moves
cover.consistency: Use one business consistently across the response, so the strategies you name are strategies that business could actually run.

concepts: the difference between a change and its result
relationships: how a named operations strategy moves quality
how a named operations strategy moves speed
how a named operations strategy moves cost
how a named operations strategy moves flexibility
accomplish: Name a specific operations strategy for each objective written about, not the objective again.
State the step between the strategy and the objective.
Keep one business across the response so the strategies are ones it could run.
Say what each strategy costs the business as well as what it gains.
requirements.syllabusSummary: Operations: operations strategies and the performance objectives they are chosen against.

coreAnswer.pattern: operations strategy → the specific change → the objective it moves
coreAnswer.statement: A business chooses operations strategies against the objectives it is under pressure on, and each strategy moves its objective by changing one concrete thing about how production runs.
explain: The strategy is the change, and the objective is the result. A paragraph that names both and not the step between them has described rather than explained.
Objectives pull against each other, so a strategy that lifts one usually costs something on another. Saying so is part of the answer.
coreAnswer.thesisIdea: Say that operations strategies work by changing something specific in production, and that the objective moves as a result of that change.
coreAnswer.acceptableThesis: Operations strategies affect quality, speed, cost and flexibility because each one changes something concrete about how the business produces, and the objective moves as a consequence of that change rather than of the intention behind it.
checklist: Each paragraph names one operations strategy.
Each paragraph names the objective it affects.
The step between the strategy and the objective is stated, not implied.
At least one paragraph says what the strategy costs as well as what it gains.

workingAnswer.base: Operations strategies affect the performance objectives a business is measured on.
workingAnswer.lead: Operations strategies affect the performance objectives a business is measured on, because

reasoning.forward: The question asks how the strategy affects the objective, so the sentence should travel from the change the business made to the objective it moved.
reasoning.backward: Your point currently names an objective and not the strategy that moves it. Say what the business changed first.

topic.direct: Name which performance objective this paragraph is about, and say that an operations strategy is what moves it.
Say that this paragraph is about how quickly the business can produce, and name the strategy that changes it.
Say that this paragraph is about what a unit costs the business to produce, and name the strategy that changes it.
Say that this paragraph is about how easily the business can change what it produces, and name the strategy that changes it.

pathways.short: Checking at each stage → fewer defects reach the customer
pathways.adds: Checking at each stage → fewer defects reach the customer
pathways.relationship: Moving quality checks into the process reduces the number of faulty units that get out of it
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that quality is decided by where the business looks for mistakes, not by how hard it tries.
pathways.whatToProve: the check moves from the end of the line into each stage → a fault is caught before more work is spent on it → fewer faulty units reach the customer
pathways.commonMistake: Saying the business improves quality by caring about quality. That restates the objective instead of naming what changed.

mechanism.text: A fault caught at the stage it is made is corrected before the next stage runs. A fault caught at the end has already passed every stage, so it leaves as finished output or is scrapped whole.
mechanism.reason: The two ends do not meet on their own: a check happening earlier does not obviously mean fewer faults escape until the middle step is stated.

topic.direct: State the relationship: checking during the process rather than at the end of it changes how many faulty units get out.

explain.direct: Explain WHY an earlier check means fewer faults reach the customer. Name the step in the middle, not the result.

ladder.text: Think about what has already happened to a unit by the time it reaches the end of the line.
Your sentence needs the middle step: what an earlier check lets the business do that a final check does not.
Say what happens to a faulty unit when it is caught at the stage it was made, and then what happens when it is not caught until the end.

pathways.short: Choosing suppliers on consistency → inputs that vary less
pathways.adds: Choosing suppliers on consistency → inputs that vary less
pathways.relationship: Selecting suppliers on how consistent their inputs are reduces the variation the business has to absorb
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that some of a business's quality is decided before anything arrives, by who it buys from.
pathways.whatToProve: the business selects a supplier on consistency rather than price alone → the inputs arriving vary less → the output varies less
pathways.commonMistake: Arguing that a more expensive supplier is a better one. The claim is about variation, not price.

mechanism.reason: The two ends already meet. Inputs that vary less produce output that varies less, and a middle step would restate that.

topic.direct: State the relationship: which supplier the business chooses decides how much variation arrives at the door.

explain.direct: Explain WHY consistent inputs produce consistent output. Say what the business no longer has to do.

pathways.short: Ordering to demand → a shorter path from order to delivery
pathways.adds: Ordering to demand → a shorter path from order to delivery
pathways.relationship: Ordering inputs against actual demand shortens the time between a customer ordering and the business delivering
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that speed comes from removing waiting, not from working faster.
pathways.whatToProve: inputs arrive against real demand rather than a forecast → less of the process is spent waiting for the right input → the customer waits less
pathways.commonMistake: Saying the business becomes faster because it holds less stock. Holding less stock is the change; the speed comes from what the business no longer waits for.

mechanism.text: Time in a process is mostly waiting rather than working. Ordering against real demand removes the wait for a forecast to be corrected, which is the wait that sits between the order and the work starting.
mechanism.reason: Holding less stock sounds like it should make a business slower, not faster, so the step that resolves that has to be stated.

topic.direct: State the relationship: ordering against demand rather than a forecast changes how long the customer waits.

explain.direct: Explain WHY ordering to demand shortens the wait. Say which wait disappears.

ladder.text: Think about what a business is waiting for when it cannot start a job.
Your sentence needs to name the wait that is removed, not just say things get faster.
Separate the time spent working from the time spent waiting, and say which one this changes.

effect.direct: Say what this achieves for speed specifically.

link.direct: Tie it back: this is one way an operations strategy affects speed.

pathways.short: Newer equipment → more output in the same hour
pathways.adds: Newer equipment → more output in the same hour
pathways.relationship: Replacing equipment with a faster generation of it raises how much the business can produce in the time it has
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing the simplest version of speed: the same hour produces more.
pathways.whatToProve: the business replaces the equipment doing the slowest step → that step takes less time → the whole process finishes sooner
pathways.commonMistake: Arguing that new technology is faster without saying which step it changed. Replacing equipment that was never the constraint changes nothing.

mechanism.text: A process finishes no faster than its slowest step. Replacing equipment only shortens the whole process when the equipment replaced was the step everything else was waiting on.
mechanism.reason: A student who does not name the constraint will argue that any new equipment is faster, which is not true and is the mistake this pathway exists to prevent.

topic.direct: State the relationship: replacing the equipment at the slowest step changes how much the business produces per hour.

explain.direct: Explain WHY this equipment, at this step, changes the whole process rather than one part of it.

ladder.text: Think about what decides how fast a chain of steps finishes.

Say what the rest of the process was waiting for, and what happens to that wait.

pathways.short: Outsourcing a non-core process → a fixed cost becomes a variable one
pathways.adds: Outsourcing a non-core process → a fixed cost becomes a variable one
pathways.relationship: Handing a non-core process to an outside provider turns the cost of running it into a cost that moves with use
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that the saving is in the shape of the cost, not only in its size.
pathways.whatToProve: the business stops running the process itself → it stops paying for that capacity whether or not it is used → cost now rises and falls with output
pathways.commonMistake: Claiming outsourcing is cheaper. Sometimes it is not; what changes reliably is that the business stops paying for idle capacity.

mechanism.text: Running a process in house means paying for the people and equipment to do it at its busiest, in every month including the quiet ones. Buying it means paying for what was used.
mechanism.reason: Cheaper and differently shaped are two different claims, and a student who does not have the middle step will make the first one, which is not always true.

topic.direct: State the relationship: moving a non-core process outside the business changes what the business pays for it.

pathways.short: Holding less stock → less money tied up in things not sold
pathways.adds: Holding less stock → less money tied up in things not sold
pathways.relationship: Reducing how much stock is held lowers what the business spends holding it
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that stock is a cost while it sits there, not only when it is bought.
pathways.whatToProve: the business holds less stock → it pays for less space, handling and tied-up money → the cost of producing a unit falls
pathways.commonMistake: Treating this as the same argument as ordering to demand. That one is about time; this one is about what holding costs.

mechanism.reason: The two ends already meet. Less stock held is less space, handling and money committed, and a middle step would restate it.

pathways.short: Designing around shared parts → a range that can change without retooling
pathways.adds: Designing around shared parts → a range that can change without retooling
pathways.relationship: Designing products around shared components lets the business change its range without rebuilding the process
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that flexibility is designed in before production, not added to it afterwards.
pathways.whatToProve: products are designed to share parts and steps → changing the range does not change most of the process → the business can respond without rebuilding
pathways.commonMistake: Saying the business is flexible because it offers more products. A wide range built on unrelated processes is less flexible, not more.

mechanism.text: What limits how quickly a business can change what it makes is how much of the process has to change with it. Products built from the same parts and steps share that process, so the change is at the end of it rather than through it.
mechanism.reason: More products sounds like more flexibility, so the step that separates the range from the process behind it has to be stated.

pathways.short: Equipment that does several jobs → capacity that can be redirected
pathways.adds: Equipment that does several jobs → capacity that can be redirected
pathways.relationship: Choosing equipment that can be reset for several jobs lets the business move capacity to whatever is being demanded
pathways.choiceMeaning: You are arguing that flexibility is a property of the equipment the business bought, and that it was paid for.
pathways.whatToProve: the equipment can be reset between jobs → capacity can move to what is being demanded → the business can meet a change in demand without new equipment
pathways.commonMistake: Ignoring what it costs. Equipment that does several jobs is usually slower at each one, and a paragraph that does not say so is arguing for something free.

mechanism.reason: The two ends already meet. Equipment that can be reset is capacity that can be moved, and a middle step would restate the relationship.

bands.text: Names a specific operations strategy for each objective, states the step between the strategy and the objective every time, and acknowledges what at least one strategy costs.
Names specific strategies and states the step for most of them. One or more paragraphs pair a strategy with an objective without saying how it gets there.
Names strategies and objectives correctly but mostly describes them rather than explaining the link between them.
Discusses operations in general terms. Strategies and objectives are named loosely or interchangeably.
Some correct terminology, without a relationship between a strategy and an objective.
